lessons.title: F and J — Your Home Base
lessons.intro: Place your left index finger on F and your right index finger on J. Feel the small raised bump on each key — that's how your fingers find home without looking down. Rest your other fingers gently on the keys beside them and keep them there.

steps.text: fjfj jfjf fjfj jfjf ffjj jjff fjfj jfjf ff jj fj jf
steps.label: New Keys — Pattern

lessons.title: D and K — Middle Fingers
lessons.intro: Your left middle finger sits on D, your right middle finger on K. Keep your index fingers anchored on F and J while you reach — don't let them float up. Return to home after every keystroke.

steps.label: New Keys — Pattern
steps.text: dkdk kdkd ddkk kkdd dkdk kdkd ddk kdd dkk kdd

lessons.title: S and L — Ring Fingers
lessons.intro: Your left ring finger reaches slightly left to S, your right ring finger to L. Your ring fingers are weaker than your middle fingers — that's normal. Keep your index and middle fingers anchored while you drill.

steps.text: slsl lsls ssll llss slsl lsls ssl lls sll lss
steps.label: New Keys — Pattern

lessons.title: A and Semicolon — Pinkies
lessons.intro: Your left pinky reaches to A, your right pinky to the semicolon (;). Pinkies are your weakest fingers and they cover the farthest reach — be patient with yourself here. This completes the home row.

lessons.title: Home Row Synthesis
lessons.intro: All eight home-row keys together. Every finger is now responsible for exactly one key. This is the foundation everything else is built on — take your time and let your fingers learn where they belong.

lessons.title: G and H — Index Fingers Reach In
lessons.intro: G is hit with your left index finger stretching one key to the right. H is hit with your right index finger stretching one key to the left. These are the trickiest keys for beginners — the index fingers have to cross the center of the keyboard. Keep everything else still.

lessons.title: T and Y — Index Fingers Reach Up-Center
lessons.intro: T is hit by your left index finger reaching up and slightly right. Y is your right index finger reaching up and slightly left. After each T or Y, bring your index finger straight back down to F or J — don't let it hang up on the top row.

lessons.title: R and U — Index Fingers Reach Up-Outer
lessons.intro: R sits above F — your left index finger reaches straight up. U sits above J — your right index finger reaches straight up. These are slightly easier than T and Y because the reach is more direct.

lessons.title: B and N — Index Fingers Reach Down
lessons.intro: B is hit by your left index finger reaching down and slightly right. N is your right index finger reaching down and slightly left — a mirror of B. The downward reach feels awkward at first. Keep your wrists low and let your fingers do the work.

lessons.title: Index Finger Synthesis
lessons.intro: Your index fingers now cover a lot of ground: F, G, R, T, B on the left and J, H, U, Y, N on the right. This drill mixes all of them together. Focus on keeping your other fingers resting on home row rather than floating up.

lessons.title: E and I — Middle Fingers Reach Up
lessons.intro: E is your left middle finger reaching straight up from D. I is your right middle finger reaching straight up from K. These are two of the most common letters in English — getting them smooth is a big deal. With E and I, you can now start typing real words.

lessons.title: W and O — Ring Fingers Reach Up
lessons.intro: W is your left ring finger reaching straight up from S. O is your right ring finger reaching straight up from L. You already know W's neighbor E and O's neighbor I — the ring fingers are doing the same move, just from one key over.

lessons.title: Words and Sentences — First Synthesis
lessons.intro: You now know enough keys to type thousands of real English words. This lesson mixes words and short sentences. Focus on rhythm and accuracy — not speed. Speed comes naturally once the movements are automatic.

steps.label: Sentence Practice
sentences: robin found an old door at the end of the long street.
it had been there for as long as she knew.
the wood felt soft and the old hinges had gone dark with age.
she tried the handle but it would not turn at all.
a bird sat on the roof and looked down at her.
the wind blew through the long dry grass nearby.
robin knew she had to find a way inside.
she would return and find a way in before long.

lessons.title: Q and P — Pinky Fingers Reach Up
lessons.intro: Q is your left pinky reaching all the way up to the top-left corner. P is your right pinky reaching to the top-right. Pinkies traveling to the top row is a long reach — it helps to let your whole hand shift slightly rather than straining just the pinky.

lessons.title: Z and Slash — Pinky Fingers Reach Down
lessons.intro: Z is your left pinky reaching down-left from A. The slash (/) is your right pinky reaching down-right from the semicolon. Both are your pinkies going in the opposite direction from Q and P. The same hand-shift trick applies — let the whole hand move slightly.

lessons.title: V and M — Index Fingers Reach Down
lessons.intro: V is your left index finger reaching down-left from F. M is your right index finger reaching down-right from J. Your index fingers already reach in many directions — this adds one more. M is one of the most common letters in English, so getting it smooth matters.

sentences: the following day robin went to the door and found an old map.
it was pinned to the post with a twist of rusted wire.
the map showed a path that ran behind the door into the garden.
robin stared at the map for a very long time and did not move.
at the very bottom of the map was a note in faded ink.
it said to push at the base of the door to get it to open.
robin pushed at the base and felt something give way inside.
she got down on her knees and began to dig away the dirt.
steps.label: Sentence Practice

lessons.title: C and Comma — Middle Fingers Reach Down
lessons.intro: C is your left middle finger reaching down-left from D. The comma (,) is your right middle finger reaching down from K. The comma is the most common punctuation mark in English writing — you'll use it constantly. These are the mirror of E and I but going down instead of up.

steps.label: Sentence Practice
sentences: robin pushed hard at the base, and the door moved inward with a soft creak.
inside, she found a garden that had grown wild for what seemed like years.
the grass was tall, the bushes thick, and the old stone path was hard to see.
she could not believe it was there, right in the town she had grown up in.
a cat sat on top of a rock and stared at her, curious but not afraid.
robin took one careful step forward, then another, then one more.
the garden was overgrown, but it was also beautiful in its own wild way.
she decided to keep the garden a secret, at least for a little while.

lessons.title: X and Period — Ring Fingers Reach Down
lessons.intro: X is your left ring finger reaching down from S. The period (.) is your right ring finger reaching down from L. The period ends sentences — and with it, your writing can finally have proper punctuation. X is rare but appears in words like next, fix, and box.

sentences: the next morning, robin brought her notebook to sketch what she had found.
she fixed the gate so it would stay open and not blow shut in the wind.
a fox had made its den near the far wall, under a tangle of old roots.
robin did not disturb the den. she just looked, then turned away.
she found an extra path that led behind the large rosebush near the back.
the path was exactly six stones wide and worn very smooth.
she wrote down everything she saw, filling six full pages by the time she left.
it was the best secret she had ever kept, and she was proud of it.
steps.label: Sentence Practice

lessons.title: All 26 Letters — Full Alphabet Synthesis
lessons.intro: You now know all 26 letters of the alphabet plus the most common punctuation marks. This lesson puts them all together. If a specific letter keeps giving you trouble, the app will suggest which earlier lesson to revisit.

steps.label: Passage
steps.text: The bright fox leaped quickly over the old wooden fence, startling a dozen birds that had been napping in the warm afternoon sun. A jazz band played somewhere in the nearby park, sending vibrant music drifting across the quiet neighborhood. Every person walking by seemed to slow down, just a little, to enjoy the unexpected gift of that sound.

lessons.title: 5 and 6 — Index Fingers, Number Row
lessons.intro: 5 is your left index finger reaching straight up from F to the number row. 6 is your right index finger reaching straight up from J. This is the farthest vertical reach on the keyboard. Move your whole hand up slightly rather than straining just the finger.

lessons.title: 4 and 7 — Index Fingers, Outer Numbers
lessons.intro: 4 is your left index finger — the same finger that hits F, R, T, G, V, B, and 5. Now add 4. Your right index adds 7 to its already long list. These are the outermost index-finger numbers.

lessons.title: 3 and 8 — Middle Fingers, Number Row
lessons.intro: 3 is your left middle finger reaching up from D and E. 8 is your right middle finger reaching up from K and I. These are directly above your home-row middle fingers — the reach is straight up.

lessons.title: 2 and 9 — Ring Fingers, Number Row
lessons.intro: 2 is your left ring finger reaching up from S and W. 9 is your right ring finger reaching up from L and O. These sit directly above your ring-finger home positions.

lessons.title: 1 and 0 — Pinky Fingers, Number Row
lessons.intro: 1 is your left pinky reaching all the way up-left from A and Q. 0 is your right pinky reaching all the way up-right from semicolon and P. These are the longest reaches on the entire keyboard — the same pinky fingers that already cover Q and Z are now going even farther.

lessons.title: Number Row Synthesis
lessons.intro: All ten digits together, then mixed with letter keys. Numbers appear in dates, addresses, measurements, scores, and years. This drill simulates the kind of mixed typing you will actually encounter.

steps.label: Mixed Alphanumeric
sentences: robin had visited the garden 14 times over the past 3 weeks.
the garden wall was about 6 feet tall and roughly 40 feet wide.
she found 3 old coins near the rosebush, from some time in the 1800s.
the fox den had 4 young kits and robin counted them from 10 feet away.
she had filled 9 pages of her notebook with drawings and notes by now.
by her 10th visit, the cat had started to sit within 2 feet of her.
robin guessed the garden had been locked for at least 30 or 40 years.
she started planting seeds in a small bed about 2 by 4 feet near the gate.
the stone path had 18 stones on one side and 19 on the other.
on her 15th visit, the fox looked at her and held still for 5 whole seconds.

lessons.title: Shift — The Opposite-Hand Rule
lessons.intro: To type a capital letter, hold the Shift key on the OPPOSITE side of the keyboard from the letter. Capitalizing F? Your right pinky holds Shift while your left index presses F. Capitalizing J? Your left pinky holds Shift while your right index presses J. This keeps both hands balanced and lets you maintain speed.

Sentences with Capitals

She had named the cat Ash, and Ash now met her at the gate every visit.

Robin spent most of that visit clearing the back corner with a small hand tool.
She found a sign buried in the dirt that read Garden of the Bell House.
Robin looked up the address at the local library and found an old article.
The house had belonged to a woman named Dr. Ford, who had passed long ago.
Robin felt that finding this place had been one of the best days of her life.

lessons.title: Capital Letters — Full Practice
lessons.intro: Capitals appear at the start of every sentence, in names, in places, and in titles. This lesson mixes capitalization throughout longer passages. If you find yourself using the same-side Shift, stop and correct the habit — it will slow you down later.

steps.label: Capitalization Drill
sentences: Robin brought her friend Marcus to see the garden one Saturday in March.
Marcus had never seen anything like it, and he stood very still for a long time.
She showed him the old sign and the article from the Nashville Courier.
According to the article, Dr. Ford had planted the garden for her students.
She had taught at Jefferson School, which had later become Riverside Middle School.
Marcus suggested they contact the school and tell them what Robin had found.
The principal, Ms. Chen, was very interested and asked to visit that afternoon.
By the end of the week, the story of the Garden of the Bell House had spread.
Robin was not sure what would happen next, but she was glad she had tried the handle.
Sometimes the best things in the world are just waiting behind an old locked door.

steps.text: Last summer, Maya and her brother joined a program at the Nashville Public Library called Reading Across America. Every Tuesday, a librarian named Mr. Okafor read aloud from a different book, and the students followed along in their own copies. One week they read from Little Women, and another week from a novel set in ancient Egypt. By the end of August, Maya had read more books than she had in any previous year, and Mr. Okafor had become her favorite person in the whole neighborhood.

lessons.title: Graduation: Pangrams I
lessons.intro: A pangram is a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet at least once. These are a classic tool for testing the full range of the keyboard. Type carefully — every key you have learned is somewhere in these sentences.

lessons.title: Graduation: Passage 1 — Animals
lessons.intro: From here on, each level is a full paragraph. You are typing real prose — the same kind you will find in books. Take your time, maintain accuracy, and let your speed build naturally.

steps.label: Passage
steps.text: The quick brown fox is perhaps the most famous animal in typing history, though it has never once jumped over an actual lazy dog. In real life, foxes are clever hunters who move through forests at night. Zebras live in vast open grasslands and rely on their bold black and white stripes to confuse predators. Every kind of wild creature, from the buzzing bee to the jumping jackrabbit, has found its own way to survive in a complex world.

steps.label: Passage
steps.text: Bright lightning bolts crack across the sky during a summer storm, and the thunder that follows can shake the windows of a whole building. Freezing wind chills the exposed skin of anyone who ventures outside too quickly in winter. Quiet snowflakes drift downward and blanket every rooftop in a soft white layer. Weather is one of the few forces that can change your plans, your mood, and your entire day without asking your permission.

steps.label: Passage
steps.text: Every great athlete knows that skill is built slowly through practice, not in one explosive jump. The best basketball players spend quiet hours working on their form before the crowd ever shows up. Boxers develop quick reflexes by training their bodies to move without thinking. Whether you play on a team or compete by yourself, the goal is always the same: push your limits, fix your weaknesses, and show up better than you were the day before.

The first computers were enormous machines that filled entire rooms and could only perform basic calculations. Today, a smartphone sitting in your pocket is more powerful than any of those early systems by a factor of millions. Programmers write code using keyboards, and the speed at which they type has a real effect on how quickly ideas become products. Learning to type well is not just a school skill, it is a foundation for almost every career that involves a screen.
steps.label: Passage
Passage
steps.text: A single oak tree can live for several hundred years, quietly growing wider and taller with every passing season. Its roots dig deep into the earth to find water, while its branches stretch outward to capture as much sunlight as possible. In the fall, the leaves change from green to blazing shades of orange, red, and gold before finally letting go. Dozens of animals, from squirrels to woodpeckers to foxes, depend on that one tree for food and shelter throughout the year.

steps.label: Passage
steps.text: Long before the age of printing, every book had to be copied by hand, one letter at a time, by skilled workers called scribes. A single Bible might take a monk years to complete, working by the light of a small candle in a drafty room. The invention of the printing press in the 1400s changed everything almost overnight, making books cheaper and knowledge available to people who had never owned one before. The keyboard you are using right now is just the latest step in that very long story.

Jazz was born in New Orleans in the early 1900s, mixing African rhythms with European harmonies in ways nobody had ever quite combined before. The music was bold, improvised, and always a little bit surprising, which is exactly why so many people loved it and so many others found it strange. Over the following decades, jazz grew into dozens of different styles and spread to every corner of the globe. Today, a quiet saxophone playing in the background of a coffee shop is the distant echo of something that once seemed revolutionary.
steps.label: Passage
Passage
steps.text: On July 20, 1969, two astronauts stepped onto the surface of the moon for the very first time, while a third orbited quietly above. The whole world watched on small black and white televisions, many of them not quite believing what they were seeing. Getting there required thousands of engineers, mathematicians, and scientists working for nearly a decade on every possible problem, from rocket fuel to space suits to navigation. It remains one of the most complex and extraordinary things human beings have ever done.

Every culture on earth has developed its own unique way of cooking, shaped by the ingredients that grow nearby and the traditions passed down through families over generations. Mexican food relies on corn, beans, and spicy chili peppers. Japanese cuisine prizes fresh fish, rice, and the quiet, precise art of presentation. In France, sauces are taken so seriously that professional chefs spend years mastering just a handful of them. Whatever your favorite dish happens to be, somebody somewhere spent a lifetime figuring out exactly how to make it taste that good.
steps.label: Passage

lessons.title: Graduation: Passage 10 — You Made It
lessons.intro: This is your final lesson. Type it through, hit your gates, and you graduate to the book library. Everything you practiced — every key pattern, every word drill, every sentence — has been building toward this.

steps.label: Final Passage
steps.text: Learning to type is, in a quiet way, one of the most useful things you will ever do. It will not feel impressive at first, but the skill compounds quickly once your fingers know where to go without your brain having to send them there. Every book you will ever write, every message you will ever send, every idea you will ever type out starts with the same twenty-six keys laid out in the same order they have always been in. You have learned them all. Now go read something.
